To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the G-CSF receptor mutation found in patients does not induce SCN or AML in the mouse.
mice carrying the mutation found in SCN and AML patients have normal granulopoiesic development and no evidence of leukemia, but demonstrate an exaggerated response to G-CSFR.
mice carrying a targeted mutation in their G-CSF receptor that is similar to that found in SCN patients have normal resting granulocytopoiesis but an exaggerated response to G-CSFR stimulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the G-CSFR in the pathogenesis and treatment of SCN and AML.

the role of mutations of granulocyte colony stimulating factor receptor (GCSFR) in the development of severe congenital and cyclic neutropenia and the subsequent development to acute myelogenous leukemia (AML).

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mutation of the G-CSFR found in a patient is not sufficient to cause a block in myeloiesis or to induce AML.
the mutation of the G-CSFR found in a patient who developed SCN and subsequently AML is not responsible for these diseases in the mouse model.
the G-CSF receptor mutation found in SCN patients is not sufficient to cause an SCN phenotype or to induce AML in mice, but that it is associated with an increased responsiveness to exogenous G-CSF.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mutation of the G-CSF receptor in SCN does not lead to a myeloproliferative disorder.
the SCN phenotype is not caused by an intrinsic defect in neutrophil survival or apoptosis, but rather a hyperprolific response to G-CSFR.
the G-CSF mutation is not sufficient to cause AML, and it is likely that the G-CS-F mutation is not the primary cause of SCN.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single mutation of the G-CSFR does not cause SCN and that the pathogenesis of SCN is more complex.
the G-CSF receptor mutation is not sufficient to explain the development of AML in patients with SCN.
